reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A mosquito-borne flavivirus spread chiefly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the same vectors as dengue and chikungunya
Most infections are asymptomatic or mild; when symptomatic, features include low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, arthralgia and notably non-purulent conjunctivitis
The major clinical concern is congenital infection: maternal Zika in pregnancy can cause microcephaly and a broader congenital Zika syndrome
It is also associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome as a post-infectious complication
Beyond mosquito bites, sexual and vertical transmission are recognised, which influences counselling and prevention
India has reported local outbreaks, so it should be considered alongside dengue and chikungunya in febrile patients with rash
Management is supportive; there is no specific antiviral therapy or licensed vaccine
Diagnosis uses RT-PCR in blood and urine during acute viraemia, with serology complicated by cross-reactivity among flaviviruses
reference.pathophysiology: Zika virus is an RNA flavivirus that, after inoculation by an Aedes mosquito, replicates in dendritic cells and spreads via lymphatics and blood. It has particular tropism for neural progenitor cells, which underlies its ability to disrupt fetal brain development when it crosses the placenta, producing microcephaly and other structural anomalies. Immune-mediated mechanisms, including molecular mimicry, are implicated in the associated Guillain-Barre syndrome. The virus can persist in immune-privileged sites such as semen, enabling sexual transmission.
infectionMimics: Acute rheumatological illness with arthralgia and rash
additionalInvestigations: RT-PCR of serum and urine during the acute viraemic phase
Zika IgM serology with confirmatory neutralisation testing given flavivirus cross-reactivity
Fetal ultrasound surveillance in infected pregnant women
Concurrent testing for dengue and chikungunya in co-endemic settings
Nerve conduction studies if Guillain-Barre syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Infection or exposure during pregnancy, given risk of severe congenital malformation
Progressive ascending weakness suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome and possible respiratory failure
Features overlapping with dengue warning signs that require exclusion of severe dengue
reference.prognosis: In non-pregnant adults the illness is usually mild and self-limiting with full recovery. The serious burden lies in adverse pregnancy and neonatal outcomes from congenital infection and in Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can cause prolonged disability or, rarely, death.
pitfalls: Assuming a dengue-like febrile rash illness cannot be Zika in co-endemic regions
Failing to counsel about sexual transmission and pregnancy risk after exposure
Over-relying on serology alone given cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses
Missing evolving Guillain-Barre syndrome in a recently infected patient
management: Manage with supportive care of rest, fluids and paracetamol for fever and pain, as there is no specific antiviral
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs until dengue is excluded, given the co-endemic bleeding risk
Prevent transmission through mosquito-bite avoidance and vector control, and advise barrier contraception given sexual transmission
Counsel on pregnancy planning and provide foetal ultrasound surveillance in infected pregnant women for congenital Zika syndrome
Recognise and manage Guillain-Barre syndrome with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange and respiratory monitoring and support
Test concurrently for dengue and chikungunya in co-endemic settings and notify public health authorities
Provide neonatal assessment and long-term developmental follow-up of infants with congenital infection
